sections.name: 西屏老街：时光的写意肖像
sections.content_zh:
西屏老街，时光的写意肖像

天蒙蒙亮，西屏老街弥漫着清冷的气息。早点店第一块门板已经卸了下来，探出一张残留着睡梦痕迹的脸。店主打了个呵欠，蹲在街边生起了煤炉，呛鼻的煤烟味在老街散发开来。

逐渐温暖的阳光将清冷驱散，阳光从尼龙遮棚的缝隙中漏下来，千丝万缕地印在老街上。紧接着，一扇扇门板啪啪地卸了下来，一卷卷帘哗哗地敞开了。

老街开始了新的一天。

北直街、人民路、横街、南直街、官塘路、塔头街、大井路、猪行路、桥亭街、济川路等组成的老街区漫溢着老照片的古旧色彩，仿佛从岁月深处踱步而出的老者，虽近迟暮却依旧鹤发童颜，依旧神采奕奕。老街完整地保存着一个古老集市的标本，它毫不犹豫地将几十年甚至是几百年前的生活无所保留地推到你面前。

老街上密布着小吃店、杂货店、打铁店、百货批发部、药店、牙科诊所、五金店、白铁店、酥饼店、光饼店、拉面店、画像店、照相馆、刻章店、钟表店、打金店、棕板店、缸钵店、花圈店、钉秤店、配锁摊、裁缝店、布店、弹棉店、鞋店、公共浴室……还有数不清的理发店和草药铺，它们就像一条拉链紧紧地咬合着。清晨的阳光仿佛一只巨手，哧啦一声拉开了老街的秘密。

老街的电杆上贴着招工信息、拍卖公告、性病广告、婚纱摄影广告和寻人寻狗启事。电线杆下蹲着一个模样古怪的小贩，身上背着一只手提播放器，播放器反复叫着：买樟脑丸、蚂蚁药、白蚁药、跳蚤药、老鼠药……这些一声长一声短的叫卖声在老街上显得特别的疲惫。算命先生端坐在太师椅上，一副对联赫然在目吉凶只在面前决，祸福无劳日后知。他端着搪瓷缸，露出了半张高深莫测的脸，正在对顾客小声嘀咕着，顾客不住地点头，点头。哧——，布店传来一声扯布声，布与空气的摩擦发出响亮的破裂声音。

一两个睡眼零星的居民穿着棉拖鞋从小巷中走出，头发乱糟糟，胡子拉碴，缩着脖子钻进了早点店。店里传出个浑浊的声音：老板娘，给我烧一碗馄饨。老板娘掀开锅盖，撒下一把馄饨籽，一只只白花花的馄饨浮在沸水上。一个围着围裙的中年男子端着一只蒸笼走了进来，包子的热气模糊了男人的脸。一笼包子顷刻一扫而光，男人转身又走进了厨房。

红太阳牌坊北侧，一家两开间的杂货店货物已经摆放了出来，一只只敞开的蛇皮袋露出了莲子、花生、橘饼、冰糖、红糖、饼干、红枣、绿豆、鸡蛋糕、桂圆、木耳、香菇、鱿鱼、虾皮、海带、笋干、萝卜片、虾米、葡萄干……身材矮小的小贩披着一件宽大的宝蓝大衣，正在忙里忙外地搬货，背后印着尽善尽美荣信味精，下面还有一行小字浙江金华。

相邻的另一家杂货店显得稍微小一些，两块门板横在一起搭成铺子，一些化肥袋和麻袋堆放在门板上，袋子中露出辣椒、红米、黑米、茶叶、生姜、大蒜、木耳……有人问这辣椒怎么卖？看店的老头拢着袖口，一只公平秤摆在他的脚尖前。他抬起了头，这是一张臃肿的脸，写满了疲惫和寂寞。老头答7块，女人说6块，老头说不行啊，我说的是实价了，女人说那就6块半吧。老头皱了一下眉头，说你要几斤？女人嘟哝了一声，这辣椒个头太小，推起自行车转身走了。

红太阳牌坊南侧，一家日用品店显得很凌乱，货品堆放得乱糟糟，皮带挂在铁丝上，像晾出一条条黑色的灰色的黄色的带鱼。鞋垫上标着一元一双，床单、被套挂着厂家直销的牌子。穿着黑色羽绒服的女店主当街敞开了衣服，将乳头塞进婴儿嘴里，婴儿吧唧吧唧地吃着奶。一个小女孩偎依在她身边，手上捧着一本《喜羊羊与灰太狼》的画册，穿花色的棉袄，是劣质的，显得很土气。三五个女孩子蹲在摊位前顾自在挑橡皮筋、发卡、头梳、剪刀、暖水袋。

百货批发部挂满了毯子、手套、耳套、蓝色的儿童保暖内衣，绣着美乐兔的内衣，印着叮当猫的羽绒衣和大头鞋，几个女人围着摊位讲起了价钱。店主是一个年轻的小伙子，他笨拙地给顾客叠着衣物，塞进一只黑色的塑料袋，一边说着，我这个价钱亏了，你到哪里都买不来的，脸上浮着一层浅浅的笑，又补了一句，出去可千万不要把这个价格对别人说啊。顾客哦哦地敷衍着。

斜对面的马路，一个年轻的女店主斜斜地挎着一只黑色的背包，眼睛看着服装，怔怔地发呆，白色的围巾耷拉在胸前，她打了个呵欠，背过身去拣起一件儿童裤，一根一根地扯去露在裤边的线脚。

人民大街一家老中医诊所里人满为患，据说他家的秘方就是祖传的，说是几百年了，具体什么时间他也说不清楚。其实也没有必要相信，几百年的时间太长，可以将繁华几度湮没成废墟，一张小小的秘方是不会有那么顽强的生命力的，即使依旧是那秘方也不见得就有多少神奇，但是祖传秘方的牌子的确让诊所财源广进。又有顾客走进他的店里，他在号脉之后和病人小声地嘀咕着，撕下一张废弃的纸片，写下了地址和电话，然后起身给病人抓药。

人民大街101号，一家百年老店，70多岁的店主叶德保全神贯注地敲打着白铁皮，一只洒水壶的轮廓在他持续地敲击中渐渐浮现出来。他的四周摆满了水桶、洒水壶、蒸笼、茶叶箱、铁畚箕……阳光从对街的玻璃上反射进店里，落在白铁上，发出明晃晃的光，一下子搅乱了阴暗的局面。一曲听起来训练有素的钢琴声从白铁店对面小巷里叮叮咚咚地传出来，使人对风花雪月有了更多的猜想。

在善应堂药店的柜台上，蹲着一只招财猫，猫绽放着灿烂的笑容，肚皮上贴着招财进宝四个金字，右手不停地摆动着。柜台上浮着一张密布沟壑的脸，透过柜台的玻璃看到一双绿色的棉鞋。一百多年了，高大的漆黑的木柜台换成了铝合金的玻璃柜台，一张张柜台后面不知道站立过多少个掌柜、伙计和员工？响起过多少次噼里啪啦的算盘声？结过多少笔账？打着手机的女孩快步从店门前走过，红色的披风仿佛一团燃烧的火焰，点燃了深沉的基调。我无端地想起这样的诗句：春风不改旧时波。
sections.content_en:
Xiping Old Street: A Freehand Portrait of Time

At dawn, Xiping Old Street is filled with a chill atmosphere. The first door plank of the breakfast shop has been removed, revealing a face still bearing traces of sleep. The shopkeeper yawns, squats by the street to light a coal stove, and the pungent smell of coal smoke spreads through the old street.

Gradually warming sunlight dispels the chill, leaking through the gaps of nylon awnings, imprinting countless threads on the old street.紧接着, door planks are removed one after another with a clatter, and rolling shutters open with a whoosh.

The old street begins a new day.

The old street district, composed of Beizhi Street, Renmin Road, Heng Street, Nanzhi Street, Guantang Road, Tatou Street, Dajing Road, Zhuxing Road, Qiaoting Street, and Jichuan Road, overflows with the antique color of old photographs, like an old man stepping out from the depths of time — though approaching old age, still with white hair and youthful face, still in high spirits. The old street completely preserves a specimen of an ancient market, unhesitatingly pushing the life of decades or even hundreds of years ago before you without reservation.

The old street is densely covered with snack shops, grocery stores, blacksmith shops, department wholesale stores, pharmacies, dental clinics, hardware stores, tin shops, shortbread shops, flatbread shops, noodle shops, portrait shops, photo studios, seal-engraving shops, clock shops, goldsmith shops, palm-fiber board shops, pottery shops, wreath shops, scale-making shops, lock-matching stalls, tailor shops, cloth shops, cotton-fluffing shops, shoe shops, public bathhouses... and countless barbershops and herbal medicine shops. They咬合 tightly like a zipper. The morning sunlight, like a giant hand, pulls open the secrets of the old street with a ripping sound.

On the utility poles of the old street are posted recruitment information, auction announcements, STD advertisements, wedding photography ads, and missing-person and missing-dog notices. Under the utility pole squats an odd-looking peddler, carrying a portable player that repeatedly calls: Buy camphor pills, ant medicine, termite medicine, flea medicine, rat medicine... These long and short hawking sounds seem particularly weary on the old street. A fortune-teller sits upright in a grand master's chair, with a couplet clearly visible: Good and ill fortune are decided before you; disaster and blessing need not be known later. He holds an enamel mug, revealing half of an unfathomable face, whispering to a customer, who keeps nodding, nodding. Rip — a cloth-tearing sound comes from the cloth shop, the friction of cloth and air发出 a loud cracking sound.

One or two sleepy residents, wearing cotton slippers, walk out of the alleys with messy hair and stubble, hunched shoulders,钻进 the breakfast shop. A turbid voice comes from inside: Boss lady, cook me a bowl of wontons. The boss lady lifts the pot lid and sprinkles a handful of wonton dough, and white wontons float on the boiling water. A middle-aged man in an apron carries a steamer in; the steam of buns blurs the man's face. A cage of buns is instantly swept clean, and the man turns and walks back into the kitchen.

North of the Red Sun Archway, a two-bay grocery store has already displayed its goods. Open woven bags reveal lotus seeds, peanuts, orange cakes, rock sugar, brown sugar, biscuits, red dates, mung beans, egg cakes, longan, wood ear mushrooms, shiitake mushrooms, squid, dried shrimp, kelp, bamboo shoots, radish slices, shrimp, raisins... The short peddler, wearing a loose royal blue coat, is busy moving goods back and forth. On the back is printed Perfect Beauty Rongxin MSG, with a small line below: Jinhua, Zhejiang.

The adjacent grocery store is slightly smaller. Two door planks laid horizontally form a shop counter, with fertilizer bags and gunny sacks stacked on the planks, revealing chili peppers, red rice, black rice, tea, ginger, garlic, wood ear mushrooms... Someone asks: How much is this chili? The old shopkeeper gathers his cuffs, with a balance scale placed before his toes. He raises his head — it is a bloated face, full of fatigue and loneliness. The old man answers 7 yuan, the woman says 6, the old man says no, I'm giving the real price, the woman says then 6.5. The old man frowns slightly and says how many jin do you want? The woman mutters that the chilies are too small, pushes her bicycle and walks away.

South of the Red Sun Archway, a daily necessities shop looks messy, with goods piled haphazardly. Belts hang on wire, like drying black, gray, and yellow hairtail fish. Insoles are marked one yuan a pair; bed sheets and quilt covers hang with factory-direct signs. The female shopkeeper in a black down jacket opens her clothes in the street, putting her nipple into the baby's mouth; the baby nurses with smacking sounds. A little girl nestles beside her, holding a Pleasant Goat and Big Big Wolf picture book, wearing a flowery cotton-padded jacket of poor quality, looking rustic. Three or five girls squat before the stall, picking rubber bands, hair clips, combs, scissors, and hot water bottles on their own.

The department wholesale store is covered with blankets, gloves, earmuffs, blue children's thermal underwear, underwear embroidered with Happy Rabbit, down jackets printed with Doraemon, and big-head shoes. Several women gather around the stall bargaining. The shopkeeper is a young man who clumsily folds clothes for the customer, stuffing them into a black plastic bag, saying: I'm losing money at this price, you can't buy it anywhere else, with a faint smile on his face, adding: Don't tell others this price when you go out. The customer responds with perfunctory oh-ohs.

Across the road diagonally, a young female shopkeeper slings a black backpack askew, staring at the clothes in a daze, a white scarf drooping on her chest. She yawns, turns around to pick up a pair of children's pants, pulling off loose threads at the pant hems one by one.

An old Chinese medicine clinic on Renmin Street is crowded. It is said that his secret recipe is ancestral, said to be hundreds of years old, though he cannot say exactly when. Actually, there is no need to believe it; hundreds of years is too long, capable of burying prosperity into ruins several times, and a small secret recipe would not have such tenacious vitality. Even if it is still that recipe, it may not be particularly miraculous, but the ancestral secret recipe sign indeed makes the clinic prosperous. Another customer enters his shop; after taking the pulse, he whispers with the patient, tears off a scrap of paper, writes down the address and phone number, then rises to fill the prescription.

At No. 101 Renmin Street, a century-old shop, the 70-something shopkeeper Ye Debao is intently hammering tinplate, and the outline of a watering can gradually emerges under his continuous hammering. Around him are buckets, watering cans, steamers, tea boxes, iron dustpans... Sunlight reflects into the shop from the glass across the street, falling on the tin,发出 a bright light, suddenly disrupting the dark scene. A well-trained piano sound comes ding-dong from the alley opposite the tin shop, making one imagine more about romance and beauty.

On the counter of the Shanyingtang Pharmacy, a maneki-neko (beckoning cat) squats, the cat blooming with a bright smile, with four golden characters Wealth Comes In on its belly, its right paw constantly waving. A face full of deep wrinkles floats above the counter; through the counter glass, a pair of green cotton shoes can be seen. Over a hundred years, the tall dark wooden counter has been replaced with an aluminum alloy glass counter. Behind these counters, who knows how many shopkeepers, clerks, and employees have stood? How many times has the clatter of abacuses sounded? How many accounts have been settled? A girl on her phone walks quickly past the shop door, her red cloak like a burning flame, igniting the deep tone. I无端 think of this poem: Spring breeze does not change the old waves.

sections.name: 鹦鹉冢：一页滑落的南宋诗笺
sections.content_zh:
鹦鹉冢，一页滑落的南宋诗笺

一张纸笺，留下惊动千年的字迹。

一口古井，见证一出爱情的盛典。

公元1657年一月的一个晚上，金陵雨花僧舍中烛光摇曳。戏剧家孟称舜终于校对完了35出《张玉娘闺房三清鹦鹉墓贞文记》剧本，他轻轻地发出一声叹息，蘸着淋漓的浓墨写下了题跋。就在孟称舜掷笔叹怜之间，我们的张玉娘借着微弱的烛光，带着一丝凄笑，从宋词中姗姗走出。

松阳县城江滨公园，在霞光的漂染下，新落成的张玉娘塑像端庄、隽丽，带着时间的仆仆风尘，颔首抚琴，若有所思、若有期艾的模样，颇有些八咏楼前李清照的风采。什么是历史？站在张玉娘塑像前便一目了然，我被压得惶惶然，那一弯娥眉，一丝笑颦，结着解不开的浓愁。张玉娘是这样的吗？也许是，也许不是。景仰者的内心，都会有一个不同的答案。

月光微，帘影晓。庭院深沉，宝鼎余香枭。浓睡不堪闻语鸟。情逐梨云，梦入青春杳。海棠阴，杨柳杪。疏雨寒烟，似我愁多少？谁唱竹枝声缭绕。欲语临风，自诉东风早。

这样美妙词句的作者，便是宋代四大女词人之一的张玉娘。张玉娘（1250年—1276年），字若琼，号一贞居士，浙江松阳县人氏。玉娘自幼聪慧饱学，博雅风华，诗词题材和风格广泛，既有风花雪月，也有金戈铁马，尤擅长古风。她的作品存世不多，诗117首，词16阕，量虽少，却将诗词的神韵写到了极致。

读孟称舜《张玉娘闺房三清鹦鹉墓贞文记》，我们看到了张玉娘人生的全景，那段遥远悲恸的往事清晰收入眼眶，直叫人惊颤不已。玉娘15岁时许配给了表亲沈佺，我没有读过沈佺的文章，但能叫玉娘以死相许的人，想必是才貌俱佳。由于是亲戚关系，相互走动机会多了，难免私下也会书信来往，传递心迹。如此恋恋风尘，两小无猜，卿卿我我，一定非常冶情。快乐时光总是如白驹过隙，后来沈家家道中落，玉娘的父亲有了悔婚之意，玉娘坚决不同意。1271年，22岁的沈佺赴京赶考，然而天不佑人，沈佺得了伤寒，病入膏肓。玉娘寄书于沈：妾不偶于君，愿死以同穴也！沈佺死后，玉娘拒绝再婚，为沈佺守节，恹恹独守空楼，度过5年悲痛的日子。

又一年的元宵节来临，玉娘面对青灯，恍惚间见沈公子出现，对玉娘说希望您不要背弃盟约。语毕，人不见。玉娘悲痛欲绝，喃喃说道：沈郎为何离我而去？不久，一代才女、情女、贞女，受尽了相思的煎熬，终殉情而死。更为感人的是侍女霜娥因悲痛忧死，另一侍女紫娥也自颈而殒，连畜养的鹦鹉也悲鸣而降。面对这样凄惨的人间景象，再铁的心肠也会为之神伤。张家沈家将沈佺、玉娘合葬，霜娥、紫娥葬在墓左，鹦鹉葬在墓右，时人称此墓群为鹦鹉冢。如今，冢前尚存一口兰雪泉井，一块残碑，昭示着南宋末年那段凄风苦雨的往事。

在我看来，文人具有常人所不具有的忧伤气质，张玉娘更是如此。她是一代才女、情女、贞女，更是绝代忧女。她心性伤感，骨子里透着冷峭，性格里闪着林黛玉的影子。自古多情伤离别，更哪堪，生离死别时。相思，相思，拦不住的相思，一个柔弱的女子，一寸寸地香消玉殒，终于青灯熬尽，撒手人寰。张玉娘死于情，亦死于文。文人向来多情，她落到了自己编织的文字罗网中，不能自拔。她不停地写出一些伤感的辞藻，聊以自慰，借以遣怀，殊不料越陷越深，整日神情恍惚，悲悲切切。文，是横在她心口的一把尖刀，不停地削弱她的生存意志，直至被自己活活折磨而死。实在叫人惋惜。若此遭遇摊在寻常人的身上，也许随着时间的推移，伤口也就慢慢愈合了，可叫玉娘摊上了，就注定了她的劫数。

江南，向来是诞生经典爱情的神祉。远一些的梁山伯与祝英台、苏小小，同时代的白娘子和许仙，稍晚一些的杜十娘，故事缠缠绵绵，多少有些传说成分。张玉娘的遭遇，是一出真实的故事，堪称江南的罗密欧与朱丽叶。现在看来，这样的故事有些俗套，但故事的主角一个是江南俊杰，一个是一代女词人，两情相悦，惺惺相惜，生死别离，这样的主角上演的爱情剧，够规格，够煽情，很有意境，很有童话色彩，自然也就不一样了。当爱被托到一定境界后，就是经典。700年的悲情，700年的守望，张玉娘和沈佺，成就了千万个爱情故事中碧玉一样的经典。

张玉娘的墓地在县城官塘门，更加准确地说叫枫树地。我时常会去走走。兰雪井，据说是当年张玉娘和沈佺幽会的地方，如今又成了他们颔颈相枕的归宿。井里荡漾着她的魂魄和春心，千秋之后，井水清冽，我们依旧能够感受到她的幽香缕缕。这样兰心慧质的女子，不多见。红
sections.content_en:
Parrot Tomb: A Page of Southern Song Poetry That Slipped Away

A sheet of paper, leaving characters that have stirred a thousand years.

An ancient well, witnessing a grand ceremony of love.

One evening in January 1657, candlelight flickered in the Yuhua Monastery in Jinling. Dramatist Meng Chengshun finally finished proofreading the 35-act play The Story of Zhang Yuniang's Boudoir, Three Purities, Parrot Tomb, and Chastity. He gently sighed, dipped his brush in rich ink, and wrote a postscript. Just as Meng Chengshun threw down his brush in pity, our Zhang Yuniang, by the faint candlelight, with a trace of a bitter smile, walked gracefully out of the Song ci poetry.

In Jiangbin Park of Songyang county seat, under the dyeing of sunset glow, the newly completed statue of Zhang Yuniang is dignified and graceful, carrying the dust of time, head bowed and hand on the qin, looking thoughtful and expectant, quite like Li Qingzhao before the Bayong Tower. What is history? Standing before the statue of Zhang Yuniang makes it clear at a glance. I am pressed into anxiety; that curved eyebrow, that faint smile and frown, tied with an unresolvable deep sorrow. Was Zhang Yuniang like this? Perhaps yes, perhaps no. In the heart of each admirer, there will be a different answer.

Moonlight faint, curtain shadows at dawn. Courtyard deep, precious tripod with lingering incense. Deep sleep cannot bear the call of birds. Love chases pear clouds, dream enters youth's oblivion. Crabapple shade, willow treetops. Sparse rain and cold mist, like how much sorrow I have? Who sings the bamboo branch sound winding? Wanting to speak to the wind, telling the east wind early.

The author of such beautiful lines is Zhang Yuniang, one of the four great female ci poets of the Song dynasty. Zhang Yuniang (1250-1276), courtesy name Ruoqiong, art name Yizhen Jushi, was a native of Songyang County, Zhejiang. Yuniang was intelligent and learned from childhood, elegant and talented, with a wide range of poetic themes and styles — both romantic and martial, especially skilled in ancient-style poetry. Her surviving works are not many: 117 poems and 16 ci pieces. Though few in number, they achieve the ultimate in poetic charm.

Reading Meng Chengshun's The Story of Zhang Yuniang's Boudoir, Three Purities, Parrot Tomb, and Chastity, we see the full panorama of Zhang Yuniang's life. That distant and sorrowful past clearly enters our eyes, making one tremble with shock. At 15, Yuniang was betrothed to her cousin Shen Quan. I have not read Shen Quan's writings, but someone who could make Yuniang promise to die for him must surely have been both talented and handsome. Because they were relatives, they had many opportunities to meet, and inevitably exchanged letters privately, conveying their feelings. Such lingering romance, childhood sweethearts, intimate and affectionate, must have been very passionate. Happy times always pass like a white colt glimpsed through a crack. Later, the Shen family's fortunes declined, and Yuniang's father regretted the engagement, but Yuniang firmly disagreed. In 1271, the 22-year-old Shen Quan went to the capital for the imperial examination, but heaven did not favor him — Shen Quan contracted typhoid and became critically ill. Yuniang sent a letter to Shen: If I cannot be united with you in life, I wish to die and share the same grave! After Shen Quan's death, Yuniang refused to remarry, kept her chastity for Shen Quan, and languished alone in an empty tower, spending five years of grief.

Another Lantern Festival arrived. Facing the green lamp, Yuniang in a trance saw Master Shen appear, saying to her: I hope you will not break our vow. With that, he vanished. Yuniang was heartbroken, murmuring: Why did Master Shen leave me? Soon, this generation's talented woman, devoted lover, and chaste woman, having endured the torment of lovesickness, finally died for love. Even more moving, her maid Shuang'e died of grief, and another maid Zi'e hanged herself; even the pet parrot cried out in sorrow and fell dead. Facing such a tragic human scene, even the hardest heart would be moved. The Zhang and Shen families buried Shen Quan and Yuniang together; Shuang'e and Zi'e were buried to the left of the tomb, and the parrot to the right. People of the time called this tomb group the Parrot Tomb. Today, before the tomb remains a well called Lanxue Spring and a broken stele, revealing the bitter and stormy past of the late Southern Song.

In my view, literati possess a melancholy temperament that ordinary people do not, and Zhang Yuniang is especially so. She was a talented woman, a devoted lover, a chaste woman, and above all a peerless melancholy woman. Her nature was sentimental, with cold sharpness in her bones, and her personality flashed the shadow of Lin Daiyu. Since ancient times,多情 people suffer at parting, even more so at life-and-death separation. Lovesickness, lovesickness, unstoppable lovesickness — a fragile woman, fading away inch by inch, finally her green lamp burned out and she left the world. Zhang Yuniang died of love, and also died of literature. Literati have always been多情; she fell into the web of words she herself wove, unable to extricate herself. She continuously wrote sorrowful phrases to console herself and express her feelings, little knowing she sank deeper and deeper,整日 in a trance, sad and mournful. Literature was a sharp knife across her heart, continuously weakening her will to live, until she was tortured to death by herself. Truly regrettable. If such a fate befell an ordinary person, perhaps with the passage of time the wound would slowly heal, but it befell Yuniang, and that注定 her doom.

Jiangnan has always been the sacred birthplace of classic love. Further back: Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai, Su Xiaoxiao; contemporary: Bai Suzhen and Xu Xian; slightly later: Du Shiniang. Their stories are intertwined, with some legendary elements. Zhang Yuniang's experience is a true story, worthy of being called the Romeo and Juliet of Jiangnan. Looking at it now, such a story seems somewhat cliché, but the protagonists — one a Jiangnan hero, the other a generation's female poet — mutually in love, appreciating each other, separated by life and death. A love drama performed by such protagonists is grand enough, emotional enough, full of意境 and fairy-tale color, naturally different. When love is elevated to a certain realm, it becomes classic. 700 years of sorrow, 700 years of waiting — Zhang Yuniang and Shen Quan have become a jade-like classic among countless love stories.

Zhang Yuniang's tomb is at Guantang Gate in the county seat, more precisely called Maple Land. I often go for a walk there. The Lanxue Well, said to be the place where Zhang Yuniang and Shen Quan secretly met, has now become their final resting place, heads resting together. In the well ripple her soul and spring heart; after a thousand autumns, the well water is still clear, and we can still feel her lingering fragrance. Such a woman with orchid heart and wisdom is rare. Red...

sections.content_zh:
陈家铺，高山之巅的栖居者

群山撕开了一处巨大的豁口，悬崖峭壁纷纷向后退去，寨头峡谷出现在了我的面前。一座连着一座山峰向目光穷及处奔跑，铺天盖地的绿化了山峰的线条，直到模糊成一片。

车子行驶在窄小的山路上，曲折而入，左弯右绕，荡上峰岭，穿越重重峡谷，毫无休止的之字形山路从山脚到山顶来回折腾着。有好事者眯着眼睛数了一下，200多道转弯。峡谷尽头，梯田、竹林、古树、山峦簇拥着一个叫陈家铺的传统村落，它隐藏在大山的褶皱里，仿佛一把半开半掩的折扇。一打开折扇，便露出了一个村落的烟火。站在陈家铺村口，深不可测的峡谷在眼界中螺旋般地向下旋转，陈家铺的脚底是一个叫庄河的村落，再往下是西坑村，再往下是下包村，一个村落一道景致，层层叠叠的景致从峡谷的底端挺到峡谷的顶端。阶梯式村落是松阳村落的建筑奇观，那么寨头峡谷就是阶梯式村落的奇观带，陈家铺村是奇观带上的奇迹。或许可以说，这是一座建在悬崖峭壁上的崖居式村落。

陈家铺村坐落在三座绵延的山冈上，远处的兆山、外围寨头尖和松路头山、左侧的龙脉山、右侧栗柴山、村后的后山将陈家铺村三面围住，只在南侧留出一个缺口，可以俯瞰到20多公里之外的松古平原。村落左侧的龙脉山犹如一条从群山中探出的龙头，非常形象和逼真，鲍氏宗祠正处在龙头上，红豆杉、香榧、杉树等20多棵古树散落在宗祠四周，宗祠前有一棵挺拔茂密的栗树，这棵栗树是村落的风水树，长势茂盛象征着村落人丁兴旺，为什么代表香火旺盛的不是香樟树，却是一棵很普通的栗树？村支书说这里的海拔有800多米，这个高度不适合香樟树生长。环顾四周，果然没有一棵香樟树。那为什么代表香火旺盛不是名贵的红豆杉呢？村里人没有人能够给出令人信服的答案。

陈家铺村北高南低的地理上构造让人有一种倾斜而下的感觉。从村落进口到最西侧，断断续续的房子绵延在500多米长的宽度上，整个村落倚靠着岩石构造的山崖，一半坡度大概有三十度左右，另外一半大概有四五十度，甚至更陡，上下高程大概有200多米，越往村落高处走，这种感觉也就越发明显。走到山顶，一朵一朵的白云从山脚浮了上来，悬浮在村落之上，也悬浮在青山绿水之上。给人一股飞翔的冲动，想要插上翅膀飞越山谷。站在山上俯瞰陈家铺村，上百幢由泥土、木板、青砖、石头建筑巧妙地利用地形地貌和岩石结构，沿着山崖、山坡一级级向下延伸，从半山延伸到山脚，一座座石头搭建而起的平台托起房屋，硬生生地在山崖上辟出了一座村落，在视野中展现出一个巨大的建筑立面，形成了壮观的阶梯式村落。红黑色相间的瓦片下压着黄色、深褐色、青色、红色、黑色、青灰色等多种色彩，形成了一个色泽繁缛的拼图，给人以强悍的视觉冲击！

由于村落依山崖陡坡而建，甚至可以称之为崖居式村落。数百年来，没有发生泥石流、山体塌方、水灾，这得益于村落的科学布局，具有极高的科研价值、建筑价值和艺术价值。陈家铺村仰仗高山的依托，以自然体现出村落的恢宏气势，是人类改造自然和回归自然的经典之作，是先民不屈精神的体现。陈家铺结合风水布局，具有浙西南淳朴的山地特色，具有山野大气象，具有朴素大美，具有浑然天成的艺术美感，深受都市人热爱，成为摄影和美术写生的乐园。

漫步在村道上，一条条纹理细密的石板道路将陈家铺村呈网状连接在一起，村道落差在几米甚至几十米不等，没有扶手，也没有围栏，如同挂在悬崖上。村道除了曲折艰险之外，有些坡度极陡，甚至有四五十度的角度，而且台阶非常狭窄，最窄的不足半米，将将一个人侧身而过。脚底下就是波涛翻滚的瓦浪，我们个个如同飞檐走壁的侠客，奇妙的行走中充满着丰沛的想象。在如此险峻的路面上行走，就不怕有什么闪失吗？从村民那里得到的却是憨厚地回答，从来没有村民走路出过事故，他们闭着眼睛也能够摸到自己的家门。此时，一个中年妇女扛着几根毛竹从山上进村，瘦小的身段压在十几米长的竹子下几乎不见踪影。趁她休息的时候与其攀谈，得知竹子重量超过100斤，她星期上山砍几次竹子，每次来回扛三趟，一天可以挣八九十块钱。

陈家铺最让我怜爱的是悬在半空中的美人靠，一截截美人靠从悬空的木板房的阳台中伸出，仿佛一把把木梳子，与它们对应的四周山峦上青丝一般的翠竹，清风吹动，翠竹摇晃，木梳临空，描摹出一番动人的情致。我见过一个画家朋友的一幅油画，一个女子靠在美人靠上，穿着一件红色的毛线，她身后的一切建筑都是虚幻的，在灰黑色彩中跳出一抹亮色，蓬勃的仪态在画面上灿然开放，她是那么地古雅，那么地恬淡，那么地精致。一幅油画让古旧的村落完全活了过来，陈家铺就是一个风华正茂的青年女子。我打听到了画面中的女子，她叫鲍淋娣，一个3岁男孩的母亲。她真的有那么美吗？画家信誓旦旦地表达了他的真诚。可惜，这天鲍淋娣去了乡政府。美人靠上不见美人，空留一帘意境，让人

Chenjiapu: Dweller on the Mountain Summit

The mountains tore open a giant gap, and cliffs and precipices retreated one after another, as Zhaitou Gorge appeared before me. Peak after peak ran toward the limit of sight, and the overwhelming green softened the lines of the peaks until they blurred into one.

The car drove on a narrow mountain road, winding in, turning left and right, swinging up ridges, crossing deep gorges. The endless zigzag mountain road tossed back and forth from foot to summit. A curious person squinted and counted: over 200 turns. At the end of the gorge, terraced fields, bamboo forests, ancient trees, and mountains簇拥 a traditional village called Chenjiapu. It is hidden in the folds of the great mountains, like a half-open folding fan. Once the fan is opened, the smoke and fire of a village are revealed. Standing at the entrance of Chenjiapu, the unfathomable gorge spirals downward in the field of vision. At the foot of Chenjiapu is a village called Zhuanghe, further down is Xikeng Village, and further down is Xiabao Village — one village, one scene, with layered scenery rising from the bottom of the gorge to the top. Ladder-type villages are the architectural wonder of Songyang villages, so Zhaitou Gorge is the wonder belt of ladder-type villages, and Chenjiapu Village is the miracle on the wonder belt. Perhaps it can be said that this is a cliff-dwelling village built on cliffs and precipices.

Chenjiapu Village sits on three rolling hills. The distant Zhao Mountain, the outer Zhaitoujian and Songlutou Mountain, the left Longmai (Dragon Vein) Mountain, the right Lichai Mountain, and the back mountain behind the village surround Chenjiapu on three sides, leaving only a gap on the south side, overlooking the Songgu Plain more than 20 kilometers away. The Longmai Mountain on the left side of the village is like a dragon head protruding from the mountains, very vivid and realistic. The Bao Family Ancestral Hall is precisely on the dragon head, with over 20 ancient trees such as Chinese yew, Chinese torreya, and fir scattered around the ancestral hall. In front of the ancestral hall stands a tall and dense chestnut tree, which is the village's feng shui tree. Its vigorous growth symbolizes the village's population prosperity. Why is it not a camphor tree that represents prosperous incense, but an ordinary chestnut tree? The village party secretary said the altitude here is over 800 meters, a height unsuitable for camphor tree growth. Looking around, indeed there is not a single camphor tree. Then why is it not the precious Chinese yew that represents prosperous incense? No one in the village could give a convincing answer.

The north-high-south-low geographical structure of Chenjiapu Village gives a feeling of tilting downward. From the village entrance to the westernmost side, intermittent houses stretch over a width of more than 500 meters. The entire village leans against a rocky cliff; half the slope is about 30 degrees, the other half about 40 to 50 degrees, even steeper, with an elevation difference of over 200 meters. The higher one walks in the village, the more pronounced this feeling becomes. Reaching the mountaintop, clouds float up from the foot of the mountain one after another,悬浮 above the village and above the green mountains and clear waters. It gives an impulse to fly, wanting to spread wings and fly over the valley. Looking down at Chenjiapu Village from the mountain, over a hundred buildings of mud, wood, blue brick, and stone cleverly利用 the terrain and rock structure, extending level by level downward along cliffs and slopes, from the mountainside to the foot. Platforms built of stone support the houses, forcibly carving out a village on the cliff, presenting a giant architectural facade in the field of vision, forming a spectacular ladder-type village. Under the red-and-black alternating tiles press various colors — yellow, dark brown, cyan, red, black, blue-gray — forming a colorful puzzle, giving a powerful visual impact!

Because the village is built on steep cliffs, it can even be called a cliff-dwelling village. For hundreds of years, there have been no mudslides, landslides, or floods, thanks to the village's scientific layout, with extremely high scientific research value, architectural value, and artistic value. Chenjiapu Village relies on the support of high mountains, naturally体现 the village's grand momentum, a classic work of humans transforming nature and returning to nature, an embodiment of the ancestors' unyielding spirit. Chenjiapu combines feng shui layout, with the simple mountain characteristics of southwestern Zhejiang, with a wild and grand atmosphere, with simple great beauty, with an innate artistic aesthetic, deeply loved by urban people, becoming a paradise for photography and art sketching.

Strolling on the village paths, fine-textured stone slab roads connect Chenjiapu Village in a network. The village paths have elevation differences of several meters or even dozens of meters, with no handrails or fences, as if hanging on a cliff. Besides being winding and dangerous, some village paths are extremely steep, even at 40 to 50 degrees, and the steps are very narrow, the narrowest less than half a meter, just enough for one person to pass sideways. Underfoot are the rolling waves of tiles; we are all like chivalrous heroes walking on eaves and walls, with rich imagination in the奇妙 walking. Walking on such dangerous roads, aren't you afraid of accidents? The answer from villagers is simple and honest: no villager has ever had an accident while walking; they can find their own doors with their eyes closed. At this moment, a middle-aged woman carries several moso bamboos into the village from the mountain, her thin figure almost invisible under the dozen-meter-long bamboos. Chatting with her while she rests, I learn the bamboos weigh over 100 jin; she goes up the mountain to cut bamboos several times a week, carrying three round trips each time, earning 80 to 90 yuan a day.

What I love most about Chenjiapu is the meirenkao (beauty's bench) hanging in mid-air. Sections of meirenkao extend from the balconies of suspended wooden houses, like wooden combs. Corresponding to them, on the surrounding mountains, green bamboo like black hair sways in the clear breeze; the wooden comb in the air depicts a touching scene. I have seen an oil painting by a painter friend: a woman leaning on a meirenkao, wearing a red sweater, with all the buildings behind her虚幻, a bright color jumping out of the gray-black palette, her vigorous posture blooming brightly on the canvas. She is so elegant, so tranquil, so exquisite. An oil painting completely brings the old village to life; Chenjiapu is a young woman in her prime. I inquired about the woman in the painting — her name is Bao Lindi, mother of a 3-year-old boy. Is she really that beautiful? The painter solemnly expressed his sincerity. Unfortunately, Bao Lindi went to the township government that day. No beauty on the beauty's bench, leaving only a curtain of意境, making one...

杨家堂，书画上的家园

清朝咸丰二年的一天，一个叫宋斤的人背着手在杨家堂一户宅院中来回踱步，过了许久，宋斤爬上梯子，提起饱蘸浓墨的毛笔，举笔向墙，只见他轻抖腕力，一排轻盈的行书落在了白粉墙上：黎明即起，洒扫庭除，要内外整洁……一粥一饭，当思来处不易……与肩挑贸易，毋占便宜。见穷苦亲邻，须加温恤……听妇言，乖骨肉，岂是丈夫，重资财，薄父母，不成人材……

宋斤写的相当轻巧，露出几许得意，跳着几分惊艳，或许在今后的日子里，让他重新再抄写百遍，再不见得可以重现眼前的经典。

洋洋洒洒，落笔生风，一气呵成，落款宋斤二字，方寸大小，简洁有力，没有一丝的拖泥带水，也没有一丝的骄揉造作。时间是次岁壬子，也就是1852年。161年后，这段文字还保留在杨家堂4号民居的门墙上。关于宋斤的记载寥寥无几，传说宋斤为了写好壁书，事先在竖立的石板上反复练笔，一天写秃一支笔方才罢休。当他登上楼梯，运笔凝神，那些烂熟于心的文字哗哗地倾泻在门墙上。宋斤只是一个很普通的族人，没有什么特别突出的事迹，让我们今天能够了解他的也就是为数不多的手迹。他到底是什么身份呢？或许是个塾师，或许是个读书人，或许只是一个农民，但他浑厚通透的笔力并不亚于一些名家，这些灌注了笔力和阅历的文字，经过他的糅合之后，以警言格句的方式赫然出现在墙头。当我琅琅诵读时，忍不住为他鼓掌，觉得宋斤离我并不遥远，他一定可以听得见我的掌声。

宋斤只是杨家堂一个普通的壁书者，类似这样的壁书杨家堂还有20多处。假如我能够摆渡到清末的杨家堂，说不定就在哪片白粉墙上遇见一个或者数个杨凝式一样的书家，他们将杨家堂的白墙当作一张硕大的白纸，行书，草书，隶书，各种书体纵情挥洒，俊逸、雄健、流美、沉郁的思笔在眼前铺排，他们的心境以书法的方式进入了公共阅读的视野。

我不懂书法，但是读懂了他们的情趣，他们在抒发性灵，一笔一趣，一书一境，举重若轻，原本是很压抑的字意在他们的化解下变得空灵轻巧。茂密的行数也不觉得拥挤，显现出众多乡野村夫的文笔驾驭能力，也显现出一派天成的真性情。一两百年后，粉已不白，一些字迹已经不清晰，仿佛氤氲的水雾从墙体上升起，浮起一朵朵饱满的祥云，满墙的墨书幻化出山隐水迢的风景。

人和古建筑之间，体验的不仅仅是物理空间，更是风雅神韵。在我看来，杨家堂倘若少了文化的神韵，纵使雕栏玉砌，纵使雕梁画栋，也缺少了品位。然而，杨家堂恰恰是一个既有华堂高屋，又是一个文养极其深的地方，无论在村落的哪个角落似乎都散发着雍容文雅的气氛。拿今天的话来说这只是一些农民书画，即使那样又何妨，那也是相当韵趣的农民书画，从本质上并不亚于一些所谓的名家。在一些村落中，好些名家的字迹事实上是后人伪托，以彰显祖先的荣耀，杨家堂人抛开这些虚荣，没有名家力作，除了宋斤之外，只有各个时期族人留下的遗墨。宋氏族人将《宋氏宗谱·家训》、《朱子治家格言》、《孝经》、《孝悌力耕》、《诗经》、《论语》等经典词句及古训搬上墙面，那些隽永飘逸的字迹，仿佛书家刚刚落笔，一转眼，书家已然骑上一匹瘦弱的毛驴穿巷而去，空留无数遐想。宋氏先祖有着长远的教育规划，以大音稀声的文字天天告诫着村民，遵守三纲五常，应当循规蹈矩，遵守礼仪之道，应当敬师重道……这是一场漫长的教化过程，像一条清澈的溪流滋养着后人，仁、义、礼、智、信渗透到了宋氏宗族子弟的心里。

4号大屋结构精致，进入外门，穿过一条狭长的通道，一转折，进入里大门，三合院，三开间，两厢房，天井宽敞，天井中铺设着三连钱的鹅卵石图纹，钱眼中镶嵌着佛教的万字纹，左右两兰花石凳上摆满了盎然开放的小花。门墙上除了书法之外还密布彩绘，右侧是一盘没有下完的棋，棋盘上似乎还弥漫着腾腾杀气，下棋者早已拂袖而去。让人猜测下棋者是谁？为何留下一盘残局。人生何尝不是一场没有对手的棋局？人的对手往往是自己，只有在迷局中顿悟，才能够走出乱局。与棋局对应的只有一棵挺拔的松树，配上贾岛的诗：松下问童子，言师采药去。只在此山中，云深不知处。又是一处此处无声胜有声的画面，谜底被主人抽走，只留下了一些无端的猜测。左侧壁画更有意思，孤零零的琴案上摆放着一把琴，琴头露在琴套外。空空荡荡的画面，又留下了一出哑谜，弹琴者是谁？听琴者又是谁？这是一出模拟而来的伯牙和钟子期的故事，门外就是高山流水，叮叮咚咚的水流声响彻于耳，难道说房子的主人在期待着知音的到来？其实，这个孤傲的主人或许是才华横溢的隐者，他以琴棋的方式表达自己的处世观。一面门墙，琴棋书画，文房四宝，体现的功能不仅仅是装饰作用，更有主人的理想和述求，表达的境界远远超过了现实寓意，让人惊叹古人浑圆的心智。

远眺杨家堂，一垛垛毗连的白墙，仿佛开放在田野中的一朵朵百合花，独立于烟雨中；檐瓦高挑轻盈，仿佛一对对舒展的翅膀，似乎在一声吆喝下便噗啦啦地振翅飞走。在众多的大屋中，6号大屋最为显眼，兀立于半山腰，几丈高的蛮石砌出一块平整的突出部，整座大屋如同骑在危岩之上。大屋为当地典型的三合院，左右两厢，中间有二层木楼。当年满墙的学报尚依稀可辨，就像贴着永恒的笑脸。天井长方形，鹅卵石铺砌的金钱状图案，蕴含金钱铺地之意。墙上十余幅以耕读渔樵、二十四孝为主题的壁画，使得大屋充满了文化气息。与壁书并列的是壁画，在宗祠、民居的墙体、大门上保留着大量精美的彩色或者黑白的吉祥图案：一对活灵活现的狮子，寓意着事事如意，母狮子伸出舌头舔小狮子，寓意着舐犊之情；有口衔灵芝的神鹿，代表着禄；还有丹凤朝阳、有福星高照、有喜鹊登梅等等，它们组成了古人心目中最理想、和谐的生活场景，使得整座老宅呈现出一派唯美的意境。

Yangjiatang: A Home on Calligraphy and Painting

One day in the second year of Qing Xianfeng (1852), a man named Song Jin paced back and forth with hands behind his back in a courtyard of Yangjiatang. After a long time, Song Jin climbed a ladder, lifted a brush saturated with thick ink, and raised it toward the wall. With a slight flick of his wrist, a row of light running script landed on the white plaster wall: Rise at dawn, sweep the courtyard, keep inside and outside clean... One porridge, one meal, think of how hard-won it is... When trading with peddlers, do not take advantage. Seeing poor relatives and neighbors, must show warmth and compassion... Listening to wives' words, alienating flesh and blood, how can one be a husband; valuing wealth, slighting parents, not becoming a proper person...

Song Jin wrote quite lightly, revealing some satisfaction, jumping with a touch of stunning elegance. Perhaps in the days to come, even if he copied it a hundred times again, he might not be able to reproduce the classic before his eyes.

Flowing freely, the brush came alive, completed in one breath, with the signature Song Jin two characters, square-inch size, concise and powerful, without a trace of dragging or artificiality. The time was the following year Renzi, i.e., 1852. 161 years later, this text still remains on the gate wall of Residence No. 4 in Yangjiatang. Records about Song Jin are few and far between. Legend says that to write wall calligraphy well, Song Jin practiced repeatedly on upright stone slabs beforehand, writing until one brush went bald a day before stopping. When he climbed the stairs, focused his brush, those words familiar by heart poured onto the gate wall with a rush. Song Jin was just an ordinary clansman, with no particularly outstanding deeds; what we can know about him today is only a few surviving handwritings. What was his identity? Perhaps a tutor, perhaps a scholar, perhaps just a farmer. But his rich and penetrating brushwork is no inferior to some famous masters. These words, infused with brush power and life experience, after his integration, appeared prominently on the wall in the form of aphorisms and maxims. When I read them aloud, I couldn't help applauding him, feeling that Song Jin is not far from me, and he must be able to hear my applause.

Song Jin was just an ordinary wall calligrapher in Yangjiatang; there are over 20 similar wall calligraphies in Yangjiatang. If I could ferry to Yangjiatang of the late Qing, I might meet one or several calligraphers like Yang Ningshi on some white plaster wall. They treated Yangjiatang's white walls as a giant sheet of white paper, with running script, cursive script, clerical script, various calligraphy styles freely挥洒 — elegant, vigorous, flowing, melancholic brushstrokes spread before the eyes, and their心境 entered the field of public reading through calligraphy.

I do not understand calligraphy, but I understand their sentiment. They are expressing their spirits; one stroke, one interest; one writing, one realm; lifting heavy as if light. The originally oppressive character meaning became light and ethereal under their resolution. Dense lines do not feel crowded, showing the calligraphy control ability of many rural villagers, and also showing a natural true temperament. After one or two hundred years, the plaster is no longer white, some characters are no longer clear, as if misty water vapor rises from the wall, floating up plump auspicious clouds, and the ink writing all over the wall transforms into a landscape of hidden mountains and distant waters.

Between people and ancient buildings, what is experienced is not only physical space, but also elegant charm. In my view, if Yangjiatang lacked cultural charm, even with carved railings and jade steps, even with carved beams and painted rafters, it would lack taste. However, Yangjiatang is precisely a place with both grand houses and profound cultural nourishment; no matter which corner of the village, it seems to exude an elegant and refined atmosphere. In today's terms, these are just peasant calligraphy and paintings, but so what? They are quite charming peasant calligraphy and paintings, essentially no inferior to some so-called masters. In some villages, many famous masters' handwriting is actually forged by later generations to highlight ancestral glory. Yangjiatang people cast aside such vanity; there are no masterpieces by famous artists, except for Song Jin, only ink relics left by clansmen of various periods. The Song clan moved classic phrases and ancient teachings from the Song Family Genealogy·Family Instructions, Zhu Xi's Family Maxims, the Classic of Filial Piety, Filial Piety and Diligence in Farming, the Book of Songs, the Analects, etc. onto the walls. Those meaningful and elegant characters, as if the calligrapher had just put down the brush, and in a blink, the calligrapher had already ridden a thin donkey through the alley and gone, leaving only endless reverie. The Song ancestors had long-term educational plans, using words of great sound but rare voice to daily admonish villagers: abide by the Three Cardinal Guides and Five Constant Virtues, should follow rules and etiquette, should respect teachers and value the Way... This is a long process of enlightenment, like a clear stream nourishing later generations, with benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and faith penetrating into the hearts of Song clan descendants.

Residence No. 4 has an exquisite structure. Entering the outer gate, passing through a narrow passage, turning, entering the inner gate: a three-sided courtyard, three bays, two wing rooms, with a spacious courtyard (tianjing) paved with three-connected-coin cobblestone patterns, with Buddhist swastika patterns inlaid in the coin centers, and orchid stone benches on both sides filled with blooming small flowers. Besides calligraphy, the gate wall is densely covered with murals. On the right is an unfinished chess game, with the board seemingly still filled with fierce killing intent, the players having long since flicked their sleeves and left. One guesses: who were the players? Why leave an unfinished game? Is not life a chess game without an opponent? One's opponent is often oneself; only by enlightenment in the maze can one走出 the chaotic situation. Corresponding to the chess game is only a tall and straight pine tree, paired with Jia Dao's poem: Under the pine I ask the boy, he says the master has gone to gather herbs. Only in this mountain, clouds deep, unknown where. Another scene where silence speaks louder than sound; the answer has been taken away by the master, leaving only some baseless speculation. The left mural is even more interesting: a lone qin (zither) table holds a qin, with the qin head exposed outside the qin cover. The empty scene leaves another riddle: who was the player? Who was the listener? This is a simulated story of Boya and Zhong Ziqi. Outside the door is High Mountains and Flowing Water, with the ding-dong sound of water resounding in the ears. Could it be that the house owner is期待 the arrival of a soulmate? In fact, this aloof owner may be a talented hermit, expressing his worldview through qin and chess. One gate wall, qin, chess, calligraphy, painting, the four treasures of the study — the function embodied is not merely decorative, but more the owner's ideals and aspirations, expressing a realm far beyond realistic meaning, making one marvel at the ancients' well-rounded mind.

Looking at Yangjiatang from afar, clusters of connected white walls are like lilies blooming in the fields, standing independently in misty rain; the high and light eaves tiles are like pairs of outstretched wings, seemingly about to flutter away with a call. Among the many great houses, Residence No. 6 is most prominent, standing alone on the mountainside, with several-zhang-high rough stones building a flat protruding part, the entire great house as if riding on a dangerous rock. The great house is a typical local three-sided courtyard, with left and right wings and a two-story wooden building in the middle. The academic notices that once covered the walls are still faintly discernible, like eternal smiling faces pasted on. The courtyard is rectangular, with cobblestone-paved coin patterns,蕴含 the meaning of money paving the ground. Over ten murals on the wall, themed on farming-studying-fishing-woodcutting and the Twenty-Four Filial Exemplars, fill the great house with cultural atmosphere. Alongside wall calligraphy are murals; on the walls and gates of ancestral halls and residences,大量 exquisite colored or black-and-white auspicious patterns are preserved: a pair of vivid lions,寓意 everything goes smoothly; a lioness伸出 tongue licking a cub,寓意 parental affection; a divine deer with lingzhi mushroom in its mouth, representing official salary; and a red phoenix facing the sun, the God of Fortune shining high, magpies landing on plum blossoms, etc. They组成 the most ideal and harmonious life scene in the ancients' minds, making the entire old house present an aesthetic意境.

sections.name: 周山头：幽谷里的家族密码
sections.content_zh:
周山头，幽谷里的家族密码

南宋末年，文林郎周梓向朝廷递交了辞呈，回到了阔别许久的家乡松阳。周梓如同困鸟出笼，远离了官场的进退荣辱，寄情于家乡的山水之中。一天，他沿着一条小溪逆流而上，来到一处四山峻壁的峡谷，只见中流一水，屈曲潆洄，周梓的目光越来越清晰生动，兴致也越来越高。曲折前行二三里许，穿过蔽日林荫，豁然见四山围出一方幽谷，谷中烟岚缭绕，一番洞天幽景。周梓惊呼奇妙！当即决定在此卜居。这片幽谷就是今天的周山头村。

明成化年间，同乡秀才叶纲用一管纤细的毛笔将周梓这次神秘行程记录在《钟山周氏宗谱》中，周梓的喜悦在笔尖的跳动中真切地浮现出来，这次行程成了翻版的《桃花源记》，或者说是《桃花源记》在周山头的重现。事实上，周山头的意境远比文字更加韵味，也更加清净幽僻。

在谷歌地图上搜索周山头，放大，放大，再放大，也就是一个小得不能再小的圆点。由于地处松阳县、武义县、莲都区三地交界节点上，地图上的周山头如同一枚图钉，将三县区地图钉在了一起，仿佛拔去这个小黑点，三县区的地图将就此散开。

周山头距离松阳县城60多公里，交通非常不便，一路尽是盘旋山道，一路满是层峦叠翠，眼前似乎出现了一只巨大的绿肺，似乎在吐故纳新之间整个人都绿了，人变成了一株养在车厢里的植物。一个半小时的车程不知不觉地过去了，村支书周火标站在路口迎接我们，他的身后是一片绝壁，脚底下传来哗哗的水流声。村口密布古树，一棵树龄350年的油杉，直径达到了两米多，需要四个壮汉手拉手才能合抱。一棵百年红豆杉根系紧紧抓住嶙峋怪石，形成了树抱石的奇景。转过一道湾，瓦浪滚滚而来，连片的屋舍就起伏在群山合抱形成的一个小洞天之中。周山头村最美的季节就是阳春三月，一片片鲜黄的油菜花，一畦畦绿油油的青茶，一簇簇粉红的桃花，接二连三的瀑布，泥墙黛瓦点缀在五颜六色之间……层次分明而又和谐搭配的色彩，如同一幅绚丽的壮观的版画。更为壮观的是万竿毛竹，苍翠欲滴，如同吸满了水汁的海绵，伸手一捋，就能捋出一把水汁。从城市走进周山头，当我从钢筋水泥的丛林中抬头，几乎一眼就认定这是自己精神的故乡。

松阳多山，许多村落以山为名，比如周山头、张山、章山、李山头、择子山……周山头村，从字义上理解就是周氏居住的山村。据族谱记载，周山头自宋末建村，迄今已有700多年历史，2013年，周山头村入选中国传统村落名录。仅从村名而言，这是一个不显山、不露水的村落，却让轻视它的人出乎意料。周山头古迹众多，巷弄曲折盘旋，墙头如群马奔腾，大屋高低林立，天井错落萦回，置身其中时失去了空间感和时间感。建筑多以清代为主，其中周氏宗祠、古戏台、周氏香火堂、白衣丞相庙、钟山书院、石拱桥等公共建筑保存基本完好，木雕、石雕、砖雕相当精细，尤以木雕为甚。

周氏宗祠镇守在村口，它始建于清乾隆四十五年（1780），与松阳大多数山村的宗祠一样，前厅后堂的四合院格局，门墙上布满了壁画，金硃红漆涂满了枋梁，一派灿然可观的景象。宗祠挂着三块字迹斑驳的匾额，分别是敦伦堂、率祖敬宗和敬酬祖德，字体轩昂，洋溢着雍容的气度。每个姓氏都有自己的堂号和对联，纪念各自姓氏的祖宗源流。宗祠大门贴着一副对联：爱莲世泽；细柳家声。爱莲是指北宋理学大家周敦颐著的《爱莲说》，细柳讲的是西汉名将周亚夫统领大军平定七国之乱，一文一武，成为周姓祖上非常荣耀的名人。据族谱记载，周质于宋绍熙间（1190～1194）由湖南道县迁居松阳县五部村，再迁鲁峰村，周质之孙周梓（1209～1266），举族自鲁峰迁居周山头村，成为周山头村周氏始迁祖。

周山头村坐北朝南，坐落在一片封闭的谷地中。由于古人认为北尊南卑，加上日照时间长，松阳绝大多数宗祠都是坐北朝南，让人惊奇的是周氏宗祠却是坐南朝北，与村落朝向正好相反。询问了多个老者，有人说宗祠是死人居住的地方，所以阴阳相反，事实是这样的吗？宗祠大门出来，向东又有一道外门，使得宗祠从形制上看起来又是坐西朝东，这就否决了老者的说法。为什么会设计成倒座形式呢？我找不到合理的解释。宗祠戏台下挤满了一张张花开一般的脸蛋，台上的是婺剧，锣鼓在戏台上锵锵锵地响着，演戏的人很认真，看戏的人也很认真，幽暗的空间中绽开着阳光一样的笑。他们都是周氏后裔，从第一代周梓算起，到他们已经是第二十几代人了。真是人生如戏，戏如人生，小山村不知上演过多少出悲喜剧。

周梓进士出身，一个以进士为起点的家族经过700多年的文养，已经演化成不折不扣的书香世家。周山头人书风盛行，礼仪有加，饱读诗书，知书达理。在多座民居的门墙上有石刻或者砖雕的题额：诒厥孙谋、气象文明、景星庆云、和风甘雨、烟霞养志等等。教育成功的一些松阳传统村落中，很多保留着私塾和学堂，横樟村保留有清代的丹阳家塾、山下阳村保留着一座清同治年的私塾、杨家堂村保存着光绪年间建造的迪德学堂、界首村保留着处州最早的女子学堂……而周山头村里至今还保留着一座钟山书院，这座悬在溪边的木板房是周氏族人教育宗族子弟的场所，那些四书五经在这里一遍遍地翻阅着，童子的嘴里熟读着圣贤经典语句。宗祠前四块立式、三座横式的插杆石，11号民居中高悬的拔元匾额，足以证明周氏先人在科举中的卓有成效。根据族谱记载，周山头村从始迁祖周梓起，共有70多人取得了进士、举人、贡生、廪生等各种功名，出仕为官者不下数十。

门的本意是封闭，它可以拒绝生人，也是对空间分割的手段之一。周山头的大门呈现出优雅、开放的方式，很少有大门是关闭的，更不要说上锁。私密的居室全部向外敞开，变成公共空间的延伸部分，村里人交往没有秘密，没有屏障，也没有障碍。大门的本意在村里发生了转变，大门的开放成为村落礼仪的标志之一。生活在这苍山野岭中，他们变得大山一样的诚实、敦厚，这些历代受到良好教化的村人知道什么是非礼勿视，什么是非礼勿听，什么是非礼勿入。族谱中对先人的评价多以：生平浑厚朴实，孝友性成，治家严肃，处世和平……和乡睦邻，济困扶危，以及修桥砌路，靡不捐资而乐成……
sections.content_en:
Zhoushantou: The Family Code in a Secluded Valley

In the late Southern Song dynasty, Wenlin Lang (a low-ranking official) Zhou Zi submitted his resignation to the court and returned to his long-separated hometown Songyang. Like a caged bird released, Zhou Zi distanced himself from the ups and downs of officialdom, placing his emotions in his hometown's mountains and waters. One day, he walked upstream along a small stream, arriving at a gorge with steep walls on all four sides. He saw a stream flowing in the middle, winding and circling; Zhou Zi's gaze became increasingly clear and vivid, and his interest grew higher. Walking曲折 for about two or three li, passing through shade-blocking forests, he suddenly saw four mountains enclosing a secluded valley, with mist curling in the valley, a scene of cave-heaven seclusion. Zhou Zi exclaimed in wonder! He immediately decided to settle here. This secluded valley is today's Zhoushantou Village.

During the Ming Chenghua period, fellow villager and scholar Ye Gang recorded Zhou Zi's mysterious journey with a slender brush in the Zhongshan Zhou Family Genealogy. Zhou Zi's joy truly emerged in the跳动 of the brush tip; this journey became a reprinted version of the Peach Blossom Spring, or rather a reappearance of the Peach Blossom Spring in Zhoushantou. In fact, Zhoushantou's意境 is far more charming and more pure and secluded than the text.

Searching for Zhoushantou on Google Maps, zoom in, zoom in, zoom in again — it is just a tiny dot that cannot be smaller. Because it is located at the junction of Songyang County, Wuyi County, and Liandu District, Zhoushantou on the map is like a pushpin nailing the three county-district maps together, as if pulling out this small black dot would cause the three maps to scatter apart.

Zhoushantou is over 60 kilometers from Songyang county seat, with very inconvenient transportation. The road is all winding mountain paths, with layers of green peaks everywhere. A giant green lung seems to appear before the eyes, as if in the process of exhaling the old and inhaling the new, the whole person turns green, becoming a plant nurtured in the carriage. An hour and a half's drive passed unknowingly. Village party secretary Zhou Huobiao stood at the路口 to greet us; behind him was a cliff, and the sound of rushing water came from underfoot. Ancient trees densely cover the village entrance: a 350-year-old Chinese fir with a diameter of over two meters, requiring four strong men to embrace it hand in hand. A century-old Chinese yew's roots tightly grip jagged rocks, forming the wonder of tree embracing stone. Turning a bend, waves of tiles roll in, and contiguous houses rise and fall in a small cave-heaven formed by the embrace of mountains. The most beautiful season in Zhoushantou is early spring: patches of bright yellow rapeseed flowers, rows of green tea, clusters of pink peach blossoms, one waterfall after another, mud walls and black tiles dotted among the colorful... Layered yet harmoniously matched colors, like a gorgeous and spectacular print. Even more spectacular are the ten thousand moso bamboos, green as if dripping, like sponges saturated with water — a stroke of the hand can wring out a handful of water. Walking into Zhoushantou from the city, when I look up from the jungle of reinforced concrete, I almost immediately recognize this as my spiritual hometown.

Songyang has many mountains, and many villages are named after mountains, such as Zhoushantou, Zhangshan, Zhangshan, Lishantou, Zezishan... Zhoushantou Village, literally understood, is the mountain village where the Zhou family lives. According to genealogy records, Zhoushantou was built in the late Song dynasty, with a history of over 700 years. In 2013, Zhoushantou Village was selected for the Chinese Traditional Villages list. Judging by the village name alone, this is a village that does not show its mountains or reveal its waters, yet it surprises those who轻视 it. Zhoushantou has many historical sites, with winding and spiraling alleys, wall tops like galloping horses, great houses standing high and low, courtyards (tianjing) scattered and winding — being inside makes one lose the sense of space and time. The buildings are mostly from the Qing dynasty, with public buildings such as the Zhou Family Ancestral Hall, ancient stage, Zhou Family Incense Hall, White-Robed Prime Minister Temple, Zhongshan Academy, and stone arch bridge basically well preserved. Wood carvings, stone carvings, and brick carvings are quite精细, especially the wood carvings.

The Zhou Family Ancestral Hall guards the village entrance. It was first built in the 45th year of Qing Qianlong (1780), and like most ancestral halls in Songyang's mountain villages, it has a four-sided courtyard layout with front hall and rear hall. The gate walls are covered with murals, and gold and red lacquer coat the beams, presenting a splendid scene. The ancestral hall hangs three plaques with faded characters: Dunlun Hall, Following Ancestors and Respecting the Clan, and Respecting and Repaying Ancestral Virtue, with imposing calligraphy exuding a graceful bearing. Each surname has its own hall name and couplet, commemorating the ancestral origin of each surname. The ancestral hall gate has a couplet: Ai Lian (Loving Lotus) world grace; Xi Liu (Fine Willow) family reputation. Ai Lian refers to the Northern Song Neo-Confucian master Zhou Dunyi's essay On Loving the Lotus; Xi Liu refers to the Western Han famous general Zhou Yafu, who commanded the army to quell the Seven Kingdoms Rebellion — one literary, one martial, becoming very glorious figures in the Zhou surname's ancestry. According to genealogy records, Zhou Zhi moved from Dao County, Hunan to Wubu Village, Songyang County during the Song Shaoxi period (1190-1194), then to Lufeng Village. Zhou Zhi's grandson Zhou Zi (1209-1266) moved the entire clan from Lufeng to Zhoushantou Village, becoming the founding ancestor of the Zhou family in Zhoushantou.

Zhoushantou Village faces south, located in an enclosed valley. Because the ancients believed north is honorable and south is humble, plus long sunshine hours, the vast majority of ancestral halls in Songyang face south. What is surprising is that the Zhou Family Ancestral Hall faces north, exactly opposite to the village's orientation. I asked several elders; some said the ancestral hall is where the dead live, so yin and yang are opposite. Is that the case? Coming out of the ancestral hall gate, there is another outer gate to the east, making the ancestral hall appear to face west-east in form, which否决 the elders'说法. Why was it designed in a reverse-seat form? I cannot find a reasonable explanation. Under the ancestral hall stage, crowds of flower-like faces are packed; on stage is Wu opera, with gongs and drums clanging on the stage. The performers are very serious, and the audience is also very serious, with sun-like smiles blooming in the dim space. They are all Zhou descendants; counting from the first generation Zhou Zi, they are already the twenty-something generation. Truly life is like a play, and a play is like life; this small mountain village has staged countless tragedies and comedies.

Zhou Zi was a jinshi (imperial examination graduate). A family starting from a jinshi, after over 700 years of cultural nourishment, has evolved into a genuine scholarly family. Zhoushantou people have a prevailing calligraphy culture, are courteous and well-mannered, well-read, and knowledgeable. On the gate walls of many residences are stone or brick-carved inscriptions: Yijue Sunmou (Planning for Descendants), Qixiang Wenming (Auspicious Civilization), Jingxing Qingyun (Auspicious Star and Auspicious Cloud), Hefeng Ganyu (Gentle Wind and Sweet Rain), Yanxia Yangzhi (Nurturing Ambition in Mist and Clouds), etc. Among some educationally successful Songyang traditional villages, many retain private schools and academies: Hengzhang Village retains the Qing dynasty Danyang Private School; Shanxiayang Village retains a Tongzhi-era private school; Yangjiatang Village retains the Dide Academy built in the Guangxu period; Jieshou Village retains the earliest girls' school in Chuzhou... And Zhoushantou Village still retains a Zhongshan Academy. This wooden-board house hanging by the stream was the place where the Zhou clan educated clan children; the Four Books and Five Classics were翻 read here over and over, with children reciting the words of sages and classics. Four vertical and three horizontal stone pole-insertion stones in front of the ancestral hall, and the Bayuan (First in Provincial Exam) plaque hanging high in Residence No. 11, sufficiently prove the Zhou ancestors' outstanding achievements in the imperial examination. According to genealogy records, from the founding ancestor Zhou Zi, Zhoushantou Village had over 70 people obtaining various academic titles such as jinshi, juren, gongsheng, and linsheng, with no fewer than several dozen serving as officials.

The original meaning of a gate is enclosure; it can reject strangers and is one of the means of spatial division. The gates of Zhoushantou present an elegant, open manner — few gates are closed, let alone locked. Private living rooms are all open outward, becoming extensions of public space. There are no secrets, no barriers, and no obstacles in villagers' interactions. The original meaning of gates has transformed in the village; the openness of gates has become one of the symbols of village etiquette. Living in these wild mountains, they have become as honest and honest as the great mountains. These villagers, who have received good education for generations, know what is not to be looked at against propriety, what is not to be listened to against propriety, and what is not to be entered against propriety. The genealogy's evaluations of ancestors mostly use: life simple and honest, filial and friendly by nature, strict in managing the family, peaceful in dealing with the world... harmonious with neighbors and villages, helping the poor and endangered, and building bridges and paving roads, all donating gladly and happily...

sections.name: 靖居：一座敞开的城池
sections.content_zh:
靖居，一座敞开的城池

站在由靖居口通往板桥的盘山公路上俯瞰靖居村，黑压压的瓦片在眼前铺排开去，如同一坨化不开的浓墨，更远的屋顶在雨气中敛藏着黯淡，已经分不出檐瓦的线条，仿佛墨汁在宣纸上洇氲而出，带着一丝余韵。陈旧的黑，安静的黑，韵味的黑，勾勒出靖居村的古旧轮廓。作为败笔，一些参差不齐的钢筋水泥建筑穿插在四处，他们将毗连的时间线索割裂，破坏了这座省级历史文化名村和中国传统村落的整体历史质感，让人不免心生遗憾。

从留下不多的线索中，我们至少可以将靖居历史追溯到宋代。靖居古称蓉川，明代改村为净居。清咸丰年间，不知何方高士大笔一挥，撰写了一副对联：靖以献无忘靖境，居以安自求居义。村民大呼此联绝妙，从此便将村名改为靖居。古有靖居村为县城出东门第一大村的说法，即便是今天，一千三百人的靖居村依旧是松阳东部最大的村落之一。靖居是由多个姓氏杂居的村落，包姓占了60%，李姓占了20%，汤姓占了15%，其他姓占5%，数百年来，他们朝夕相处，和睦地生活在这个自成体系的区域中。

靖居村坐落于松阳县城通往处州府城古驿道的要冲之处，龙丽公路贯通后，古驿道一夜之间冷却下来，靖居成为被遗忘的角落。八十年代撤销了靖居乡，成立了象溪镇，从此靖居又从乡政府所在地降格为一个行政村。或许正是这样，靖居村的格局才得以基本完整地保留下来。虽然，靖居没有奢华的豪宅，也没有气势高大的城垣，它的布局却近乎完美。门前山、端山、祠堂山、白碧桥山围成一块并不宽阔的谷地，靖居村就坐落在谷地中央，形成一个独立的地理单元。左右两侧低矮而绵延的山峰如同一双缓缓伸展的手臂，将靖居村紧紧地环抱在胸。小山的外围依然是榛莽的山峦，形成高大的屏风拱卫着村落，它们隐匿在无边的雨雾中完全失去了形状。

村民主任包荣强说靖居村中间大，两头小，如同一艘由南向北航行的船，船头朝向端山，船尾朝向白碧桥。记得距离村口还有一段距离的水口处，把守着一道筑于清代的堤坝，坝高十余米，顶宽四米，长百余步，13棵香樟、糙树、苦槠等大树如同篱笆一样扎在堤坝上，那些看的见和看不见的根系牢牢地抓住堤坝。树群已逾数百年，有的高达二三十米，树荫参天，已成为了古村一景。一般村落的水口要么簇拥着成片的密林，要么对峙山峰形成狮象把关的格局，这种一排整齐的大树排列的格局显得相当奇特，除了巩固堤坝之外，具体还能起到什么作用？这种布局很难让人参透，留下了丰富的想象空间。经过包荣强的介绍，我立即想起了这排大树如同码头的木桩，为这艘船用来维系想象中的缆绳。有了缆绳，才可以让这艘大船随时停靠下来，不会漂泊无依。

靖居虽说是村，建筑格局类似于一座城池。从军事防御的角度看，中国古代城池构筑有城墙、城楼、城门和护城河，可谓布局精妙，机关重重，但是靖居没有防御体系，外围四座小山形成意象中的四面城墙，南方辟出一面旷地，一排茂密的大树种植于此，如同藩篱，堵住了村落的豁口，形成了意象中的城门。东西各有一条溪流如同护城河一样从村落两侧淌过，两条清澈的溪流让村落的灵性在水影中悉数袒露。再外围，还是一层一层的大山，城垣一样包围着村落。山峰，溪流，村落，田地，树木，靖居构筑出自成体系的区域，如同一座敞开的城池。

从松阳县城通往处州府城的蓉川古驿道穿村而过，与南北走向的街道在村中交汇，形成一个不规则的十字街，组成村落的中轴线。几十条纵横的巷道在街道两侧散开，里边矗立着40多幢明清风格的民居群。进入老街后，我完全陷入了不知今昔是何年的时光恍惚。一里长的街道列肆如栉，保留着旅馆、南货店、染坊、中药店、理发店等十数间老店铺，还保留着一座残败的古驿站，老街印证了靖居曾经是个发达商埠的前身。明洪武年间，官府在这条驿道上设立巡检司，盘查过往行人、缉拿奸细、稽查无路引外出之人、截获脱逃军人及囚犯、打击走私，维护正常的商贸往来。巡检司是卫所制的补充，兼具派出所的功能，维护地方治安，甚至可以审理普通案件。如今，巡检司湮没在了历史的云烟深处，老街也冷冷清清，只有少数几家店铺还在营业。

古代城池建有行政管理机构衙门、祭祀孔子的文庙、祭祀关公的武庙、祭祀城隍爷的城隍庙、城市的文教设施书院等官方建筑，城内道路以联系各向城门的街道为主，两侧坐落着店铺和民居，构成完整的城池布局。靖居村虽然缺少衙门，但历代在此设有驿站，明代曾经设有巡检司；虽然没有城隍庙，但是村东有社庙；虽然没有文庙，但村口有文昌阁和关帝庙；靖居村早年有蓉川书院，是地方文脉所在，培育了大批文化精英；村西北有祥云寺，东南边有道观东山尖，村中有夫人桥，村南有夫人殿，村落南北各有一座水碓，城池公共建筑这里应有尽有，只是规格较县城降低了许多，格局也缩小了许多。它们虽然不是村落标志性建筑，但是井然有序地分布在村落各处，数百年来一直发挥着自己的功能。不是城池，却具备城池的雏形，从布局中隐隐透露出靖居先人的心机，一代代人持之以恒地建起一座微型城邑，并一直将古老的格局保留到了今天。

靖居村矗立着许多闪烁着徽派光环的建筑，马头墙林立，小青瓦覆顶，三合院、四合院的两层泥墙木结构楼房。高大的马头墙在仰头的瞬间要来一些过渡，墙体上勾满了祥云，黑瓦排成的马头墙缓缓向天探出它的棱角，如同大鹏展开的翅膀，具有飞翔的力感。与徽派建筑的砖木结构不一样的是，这些的建筑多为泥木结构。由于泥墙比砖墙更加厚实稳重，这些建筑显得比徽派建筑更加雄浑挺拔，特别是在斜风细雨中，那些湿漉漉的墙垣

Jingju: An Open City

Standing on the winding mountain road from Jingjukou to Banqiao, overlooking Jingju Village, dark tiles spread before the eyes like a lump of thick ink that cannot be dissolved. More distant roofs conceal their dimness in the misty rain, and the lines of eaves and tiles can no longer be distinguished, as if ink has seeped out on rice paper, carrying a trace of lingering charm. Old black, quiet black, charming black — these outline the ancient silhouette of Jingju Village. As flaws, some uneven reinforced concrete buildings are interspersed everywhere, severing the connected thread of time, destroying the overall historical texture of this provincial historical and cultural village and Chinese traditional village, making one inevitably feel regret.

From the few clues left, we can at least trace Jingju's history back to the Song dynasty. Jingju was anciently called Rongchuan, and in the Ming dynasty the village was renamed Jingju (Pure Dwelling). During the Qing Xianfeng period, an unknown master wrote a couplet with a grand stroke: Jing (peace) to offer without forgetting the peaceful realm; Ju (dwelling) to settle and seek the righteousness of dwelling. Villagers exclaimed that this couplet was marvelous, and from then on changed the village name to Jingju. There is an ancient saying that Jingju Village was the largest village east of the county seat's east gate. Even today, Jingju Village with 1,300 people remains one of the largest villages in eastern Songyang. Jingju is a village inhabited by multiple surnames: the Bao surname accounts for 60%, Li 20%, Tang 15%, and other surnames 5%. For hundreds of years, they have lived together day and night, harmoniously in this self-contained region.

Jingju Village is located at the strategic point of the ancient post road from Songyang county seat to Chuzhou prefecture city. After the Longli Highway opened, the ancient post road cooled down overnight, and Jingju became a forgotten corner. In the 1980s, Jingju Township was撤销 and Xiangxi Town was established, and from then on Jingju was downgraded from a township government seat to an administrative village. Perhaps precisely because of this, Jingju Village's layout was basically completely preserved. Although Jingju has no luxurious mansions and no imposing city walls, its layout is nearly perfect. Menqian Mountain, Duanshan, Citang Mountain, and Baibiqiao Mountain enclose a not-too-broad valley, and Jingju Village sits in the center of the valley, forming an independent geographical unit. The low and rolling mountains on both left and right sides are like slowly stretching arms, tightly embracing Jingju Village. Beyond the small hills are still wild mountains, forming tall screens guarding the village, hidden in the boundless mist and rain, completely losing their shape.

Village director Bao Rongqiang said Jingju Village is large in the middle and small at both ends, like a ship sailing from south to north, with the bow facing Duanshan and the stern facing Baibi Bridge. I remember that at the water mouth some distance from the village entrance, a dam built in the Qing dynasty guards the way. The dam is over ten meters high, four meters wide at the top, and over a hundred paces long. Thirteen large trees such as camphor,糙 tree, and sawtooth oak扎 into the dam like fences; their visible and invisible roots firmly grip the dam. The tree group is over several hundred years old, some 20 to 30 meters high, with towering shade, already becoming a scene of the ancient village. Generally, a village's water mouth is either surrounded by dense forests or flanked by mountains forming a lion-elephant gate pattern. This pattern of a row of neatly arranged trees is quite peculiar. Besides consolidating the dam, what specific function does it serve? This layout is hard to decipher, leaving rich imaginative space. After Bao Rongqiang's introduction, I immediately thought of this row of trees as dock pilings, used to tie the imagined mooring rope for this ship. With a mooring rope, this great ship can dock at any time, not drifting helplessly.

Although Jingju is a village, its architectural layout is similar to a city. From a military defense perspective, ancient Chinese cities were constructed with city walls, towers, gates, and moats — a sophisticated layout with numerous mechanisms. But Jingju has no defense system. Four surrounding small hills form the imagined four-sided city walls; to the south, an open space is辟 out, with a row of dense trees planted there, like a fence, blocking the village's gap and forming the imagined city gate. On the east and west, a stream each flows past both sides of the village like a moat. The two clear streams fully reveal the village's spirituality in the water reflections. Beyond that, still layers of mountains, like city walls surrounding the village. Mountains, streams, village, fields, trees — Jingju constructs a self-contained region, like an open city.

The Rongchuan Ancient Post Road from Songyang county seat to Chuzhou prefecture city passes through the village, intersecting with the north-south street in the village center, forming an irregular cross street that constitutes the village's central axis. Dozens of crisscrossing alleys spread out on both sides of the street, with over 40 Ming-Qing style residence clusters standing inside. Entering the old street, I completely fell into a time trance of not knowing what year it is. The one-li-long street is lined with shops, preserving over ten old shops such as inns, south-goods stores, dye workshops, Chinese medicine pharmacies, and barbershops, as well as a dilapidated ancient post station. The old street confirms Jingju's past as a developed commercial port. During the Ming Hongwu period, the government established a xunjiansi (inspection office) on this post road, to check passing travelers, apprehend spies, inspect those leaving without travel permits, intercept escaped soldiers and prisoners, crack down on smuggling, and maintain normal commercial exchanges. The xunjiansi was a supplement to the weisuo (military guard) system,兼具 the function of a police station, maintaining local public order, and even able to hear ordinary cases. Today, the xunjiansi has sunk into the clouds of history, and the old street is also desolate, with only a few shops still operating.

Ancient cities had official buildings such as administrative yamen, Confucian temples for sacrificing Confucius, martial temples for sacrificing Guan Yu, city god temples for sacrificing the city god, and cultural-educational facilities such as academies. City roads were mainly streets connecting gates in all directions, with shops and residences on both sides,构成 a complete city layout. Although Jingju Village lacks a yamen, post stations were established here in various dynasties, and a xunjiansi was set up in the Ming dynasty; although there is no city god temple, there is a community temple east of the village; although there is no Confucian temple, there are a Wenchang Pavilion and Guandi Temple at the village entrance; Jingju Village early had the Rongchuan Academy, the center of local cultural lineage, cultivating a large number of cultural elites; northwest of the village is Xiangyun Temple, southeast is the Daoist temple Dongshanjian, in the village is Furen Bridge, south of the village is Furen Hall, and north and south of the village each has a water-powered trip hammer (shuidui). City public buildings are all here, just at a lower规格 than the county seat and with a smaller layout. Although they are not village landmark buildings, they are distributed in an orderly manner throughout the village, performing their functions for hundreds of years. Not a city, yet possessing the雏形 of a city, the layout subtly reveals the ingenuity of Jingju's ancestors. Generation after generation persistently built a miniature city, and has preserved the ancient layout to this day.

Jingju Village stands with many buildings闪烁 with Huizhou-style aura: horse-head walls stand in rows, small gray tiles cover roofs, two-story mud-wall wooden-structure buildings in three-sided and four-sided courtyard compounds. The tall horse-head walls, when looked up at, require some transition; the walls are filled with auspicious clouds, and the horse-head walls of black tiles slowly protrude their edges toward the sky, like a great roc spreading its wings, with a sense of flying power. Unlike the brick-wood structure of Huizhou architecture, these buildings are mostly mud-wood structures. Because mud walls are thicker and more stable than brick walls, these buildings appear more vigorous and upright than Huizhou architecture, especially in slanting wind and drizzling rain, those wet walls...

sections.name: 章山：莲花宝座上的福祉
sections.content_zh:
章山，莲花宝座上的福祉

北纬28度20分，东经119度24分，在这个狭小的区域中藏纳着一座玄妙的小山村。一条面条一样窄小的山路荡上峰岭，穿越四合山壁，转过二十多道弯，曲折而入，就来到了名不见经传的裕溪乡章山村。章山村落在山坳中，如同另辟一个寰界，带着些许不为人知的高深意境。

章山村得名于章山寺。章山寺是当年丽水与松阳交界处的一座古寺，庙宇高大，信徒众多，香火鼎盛。我们已无从追溯章山寺的开山历程，建于何时，毁于何时，以及深藏期间的历史，一切均无记载。寺庙存有一亩见方的墙基遗址和钟楼旧址，一只石香炉孤立在残垣断壁中显得相当地突兀，属于章山寺的故事已经沉淀在遗址中，昔日的红砖碧瓦已经被草木的狂野给遮蔽了，只剩下了一则远古的神话跳跃在章山人温暖的舌尖之上。

章山的风水早在若干年前就引起僧人的注意，并在此建寺，但真正成为一座村落却要等到清康熙末年。一天，一个叫吕祖富的碧湖保定人来到章山寺上香，这个年轻人正为分家后无处安身而苦恼，他想在章山寺烧香许愿，为他安身寻找一处上佳的居所。僧人将吕祖富带到了章山寺北一里开外的一处山谷，指了指一块长弧形的谷地，没有留下一句话就转身离去。吕祖富环顾了这块郁郁葱葱的土地，似有开窍，于是在僧人所指处搭起了一座茅屋，这个家徒四壁的年轻人在此开始了艰辛的扎根创业。没有人知道他为什么选择了章山村作为落脚点，俗话说寺庙道观占尽天下好风水，或许他在僧人的指点下豁然顿悟，或许他一眼就相中了此处山环水抱的清净地域。章山真正意义上的惊艳亮相，竟然缘起于一次上香，在之后的三百年间，吕氏家族渐渐繁衍兴旺，几十幢规模不一的屋舍沿着狭长的山谷铺开，形成今天我们所看到的层次明朗的章山村。

三百年后的一个秋天，我沿着吕祖富当年上山的道路进入了章山村，前夜刚刚下了一场饱雨，周遭的山色经过洗涤，显得特别鲜亮，更远处的章山谷地云蒸霞蔚，让人联想到只在此山中，云深不知处的意境。秋天是章山一年最好的时节，满山的板栗树泛着青光，枫叶透着霞光色泽，里里外外色彩斑斓。还没有到达村落，远远就听到哗哗的水响声，车子经过几折回转，一条几十米高的瀑布飞溅而下，铺成细细的纹理，像丝绸，像一层薄薄的轻纱，披在石头上，扯出无数的细帘。岩石表面布满青苔，绿滋滋，娇滴滴，亮着一层水渍，像极了丝绸的缎边。瀑布四周植被在水色的滋润下特别地葳蕤茂盛，绿色沿着岩石发散开去，原本沉重如铁的山体刹那间变得轻逸。飞泻的瀑布，飘洒的水汽，潮润的空气，植被的氤氲气息，整个山野弥漫着一丝甜丝丝的味道。

接待我的村民叫吕丽伟，一个46岁的中年汉子，一脸的笑意，如同村口盛开的百年桂花树。我们在这个不大的村子里悠转，章山村和松阳其他传统村落并无两样，古老民居完整地保留着清代的建筑格局和风貌，而且独具山地建筑特色，块石垒砌成几米高的墙基，统一的土墙老房子依照山形逐次排开，呈现出宽大的扇面，那些鲜艳的黄色在满山翠绿中显得格外夺目。一条环状块石路将章山村连接在一起，如同一条溯流而上的时间长河，章山村时光浓缩在了这短短的几百米的逼仄村道上，我们一级级向上，仿佛穿越了三百年。横梁、门窗、门楣上的精美木雕和砖雕，无外乎是福寿的美好期盼，村落中没有彰显富贵气，却处处透显出章山人小富即安的满足。吕氏祖先有着精明的经商头脑，他们种植和营销油茶，最兴盛之时，通过陆路将油茶推销到金华，通过水路将油茶推销到丽水和温州，至今在村头还坐落着一座榨油坊，仿佛还在印证着当年的辉煌往事。章山村大屋虽然大都已经破落，祖先的牌位还在供桌上坚韧地挺立着，一缕缕香烟依旧绵延不绝，吕氏子孙还是保持着传统的以孝持家之风，保持着恭俭谦让的风气，每逢重要节气和祖先祭日总是香火不断，这正是章山人保持了数百年的耕读之风和宗族良好的教化之功。

整个章山村的布局，自始至终围绕着一个藏字。章山村藏在距离龙丽省道5里的山坳中，三面环山，一面豁口正对着松阴溪，这样的布局隐隐让我寻到了风水的存在，总觉得此处藏在一个天大的秘密，但是一切并不明晰。我想在建筑和山野间寻找一些不寻常处，走遍了整个村落依旧毫无头绪，仿佛村落所有的故事已经在时间中消磨干净，真有种不识庐山真面目，只缘身在此山中的感慨。正当我即将失望时，谷地中心的圆形山丘引起了我的注意，它的轮廓丰满而又圆润，密布丰茂的树木，我和吕丽伟拔开半人高的野草，一脚深一脚浅地登上这个并不高大的山丘。

站在山顶向四处眺望，大块大块的云朵堆满了天空，很快在风中走散，四周苍莽群山飘来眼底，一溜溜山体轮廓起起伏伏，勾勒出一幅无比空灵的画面。山体的伸展是豪放的，潇洒地跌宕而去，山体褶皱的连接部分是婉约的，甚至有些婀娜，一动一静，一张一敛，章山让我看到了太极，一种道家气场弥漫在整个谷地。我没有学过风水堪舆之术，但是我有着一双辨识村落格局的眼力，我坚信看到了一幅玄妙的奇景，以脚下的山丘为圆心，前后左右摊开了形如莲瓣的山峰，组成一朵完整的莲花。以前对古人为什么使用一朵朵来形容山峰感到困惑，今天在一个特定的场景中终于一眼顿悟。此时，我如站莲台，仿佛脚踏莲心，双手自然地就合十了。

当我指出此处是莲花时，同去的几个章山人开始议论起来，吕丽伟曾经查过族谱，吕祖富的曾祖父明伦公曾任松阳县尉（相当于分管公检法的副县长），死后就葬在章山赤路圩自然村，后人称之为莲花坟。另一个老者说在村落北部，也坐落着一座祖坟，当地人称之为莲花根。他们的说法和我的看法对应了，这的的确确是一朵盛开的莲花，它正含笑地迎接着后人对它的认识。

圆丘是最佳观景点，360度大回转，不同角度涌现出不同的景致，章山之美，被神秘气息一一笼罩。浮云一朵朵飘摇在头顶，我会幻想我所站的位置，正是当年吕祖富所站的位置，我可以想象，当吕祖富一不小心窥见了章山隐蔽在天地之间的秘密时，那一刻洋溢在他脸上必定是如痴如醉的表情。我还看到了一张张吕祖富后人的脸，他们欣喜，惊异，满脸洋溢着对祖先的崇敬之情。如果真有造物主，对于章山，他的手笔是艺术化的，一定非常慷慨大方，这是一个可以和横樟、杨家堂风水相媲美的地方，从形态上而言，或许更相似。许多地方的地形地貌展示的

Zhangshan: Blessing on the Lotus Throne

At 28 degrees 20 minutes north latitude, 119 degrees 24 minutes east longitude, in this narrow region hides a mysterious small mountain village. Noodle-like narrow mountain roads swing up ridges, crossing enclosed mountain walls, turning over twenty-some bends, winding in — and one arrives at the little-known Zhangshan Village in Yuxi Township. Zhangshan Village sits in a mountain hollow, as if creating another world, with some unfathomable profound meaning.

Zhangshan Village takes its name from Zhangshan Temple. Zhangshan Temple was an ancient temple at the border of Lishui and Songyang, with tall temple buildings, many believers, and prosperous incense. We can no longer trace Zhangshan Temple's founding history — when it was built, when it was destroyed, and the history hidden within — all unrecorded. The temple has a one-mu square wall foundation site and bell tower ruins, with a stone incense burner standing isolated among the ruined walls, quite突兀. The stories belonging to Zhangshan Temple have settled in the ruins; the former red bricks and green tiles have been遮蔽 by the wildness of vegetation, leaving only an ancient myth jumping on the warm tongues of Zhangshan people.

Zhangshan's feng shui caught the attention of monks several hundred years ago, who built a temple here, but it truly became a village only in the late Qing Kangxi period. One day, a man named Lü Zufu from Baoding, Bihu, came to Zhangshan Temple to burn incense. This young man was distressed about having no place to settle after family division; he wanted to make a wish at Zhangshan Temple to find an excellent place to live. A monk led Lü Zufu to a valley one li north of Zhangshan Temple, pointed to a long arc-shaped valley, and turned away without a word. Lü Zufu looked around this lush land, seemed to have an epiphany, and built a thatched hut at the place the monk pointed out. This young man with nothing began his hard struggle to take root here. No one knows why he chose Zhangshan Village as his foothold. As the saying goes, temples and Taoist temples occupy the best feng shui under heaven; perhaps he suddenly realized under the monk's guidance, or perhaps he immediately took a fancy to this clean place surrounded by mountains and waters. Zhangshan's truly stunning debut actually originated from an incense-burning visit. In the following three hundred years, the Lü family gradually multiplied and prospered, with dozens of houses of varying sizes spreading along the narrow valley, forming today's clearly layered Zhangshan Village.

One autumn three hundred years later, I entered Zhangshan Village along the road Lü Zufu took up the mountain. A heavy rain had fallen the night before, and the surrounding mountain colors, washed clean, appeared particularly bright; the more distant Zhangshan valley was shrouded in clouds and mist, reminding one of the意境 only in this mountain, clouds deep, unknown where. Autumn is the best season of the year in Zhangshan. The chestnut trees all over the mountain glow with green light, and maple leaves show sunset colors, colorful inside and out. Before reaching the village, the sound of rushing water was heard from afar. After several turns, a waterfall dozens of meters high splashed down,铺成 fine textures, like silk, like a thin gauze, draped over the stones, pulling out countless thin curtains. The rock surface is covered with moss, green and tender, shining with a layer of water stains, exactly like the satin edge of silk. The vegetation around the waterfall is particularly lush under the nourishment of water, with green spreading along the rocks, and the originally iron-heavy mountain body suddenly became light. The cascading waterfall, drifting water vapor, moist air, and dense vegetation atmosphere fill the entire mountain wilderness with a sweet taste.

The villager receiving me is Lü Liwei, a 46-year-old middle-aged man with a smiling face, like the century-old osmanthus tree blooming at the village entrance. We wandered around this not-large village. Zhangshan Village is no different from other traditional villages in Songyang: ancient residences completely preserve the Qing dynasty architectural layout and style, and uniquely feature mountain architecture. Block stones are piled into several-meter-high wall foundations, and the uniform earthen-wall old houses are arranged in sequence according to the mountain shape, presenting a broad fan surface. Those bright yellows stand out particularly among the mountain green. A ring-shaped block-stone road connects Zhangshan Village, like a time river flowing upstream. Zhangshan's time is浓缩 in these few hundred meters of narrow village road; as we climb step by step, it is as if穿越 three hundred years. The exquisite wood carvings and brick carvings on beams, doors, windows, and lintels are nothing more than美好 expectations of fortune and longevity. The village does not show off wealth, but everywhere reveals the contentment of Zhangshan people with moderate prosperity. The Lü ancestors had shrewd business minds; they planted and marketed oil-tea camellia. At its peak, they sold oil-tea camellia to Jinhua by land and to Lishui and Wenzhou by water. To this day, an oil press workshop still sits at the village head, as if still confirming the glorious past. Although most of Zhangshan's great houses are now dilapidated, ancestral tablets still stand坚韧 on the offering tables, with wisps of incense still continuing. Lü descendants still maintain the traditional tradition of managing the family with filial piety, maintaining a respectful and modest风气, with incense always burning during important festivals and ancestral sacrifice days. This is precisely the result of Zhangshan people maintaining hundreds of years of farming-studying ethos and good clan enlightenment.

The entire layout of Zhangshan Village revolves around the word hidden (cang) from beginning to end. Zhangshan Village is hidden in a mountain hollow 5 li from the Longli Provincial Highway, surrounded by mountains on three sides, with one opening facing the Songyin River. This layout faintly让 me find the existence of feng shui, always feeling that a huge secret is hidden here, but everything is unclear. I wanted to find something unusual in the buildings and mountains, but after walking the entire village I still had no clue, as if all the village's stories have been worn away in time, truly with the feeling of not knowing the true face of Lushan, only because one is in this mountain. Just as I was about to be disappointed, the circular hill in the center of the valley caught my attention. Its outline is full and round, densely covered with lush trees. Lü Liwei and I pushed aside waist-high weeds and climbed this not-tall hill, one foot deep and one foot shallow.

Standing on the hilltop looking around, large blocks of clouds filled the sky, quickly dispersing in the wind. The surrounding vast mountains floated before my eyes, with rolling mountain outlines sketching an incomparably ethereal picture. The mountain's extension is bold, flowing down freely; the connecting parts of the mountain's folds are graceful, even somewhat charming. One movement and one stillness, one expansion and one contraction — Zhangshan让 me see Taiji, a Taoist aura permeating the entire valley. I have not studied feng shui and geomancy, but I have an eye for identifying village layouts. I firmly believe I saw a mysterious wonder: with the hill underfoot as the center, peaks shaped like lotus petals spread out in front, back, left, and right, forming a complete lotus. I used to be puzzled by why the ancients used blossoms to describe mountain peaks, but today in a specific scene I finally understood at a glance. At this moment, I am as if standing on a lotus platform, as if stepping on the lotus heart, with hands naturally joined in prayer.

When I pointed out that this place is a lotus, several Zhangshan people who came with me began to discuss. Lü Liwei had once checked the genealogy: Lü Zufu's great-grandfather Minglun Gong served as Songyang County Magistrate (equivalent to a deputy county magistrate in charge of public security, procuratorate, and court), and after death was buried in Chiluwei Natural Village of Zhangshan, later called Lotus Grave by descendants. Another old man said that in the northern part of the village, there is also an ancestral grave, locally called Lotus Root. Their说法 corresponds with my view: this is indeed a blooming lotus, smilingly welcoming later generations' recognition of it.

The round hill is the best viewing point, with a 360-degree full rotation, different angles presenting different scenery. The beauty of Zhangshan is shrouded one by one by mysterious atmosphere. Floating clouds drift overhead one by one. I would imagine that the position I stand is exactly where Lü Zufu once stood. I can imagine that when Lü Zufu accidentally glimpsed the secret of Zhangshan hidden between heaven and earth, the expression on his face at that moment must have been intoxicated. I also saw the faces of Lü Zufu's descendants — they are delighted, amazed, their faces full of reverence for their ancestors. If there truly is a Creator, for Zhangshan, his brushwork is artistic and must be very generous. This is a place comparable to the feng shui of Hengzhang and Yangjiatang; in terms of form, perhaps even more similar. The topography of many places displays...

sections.name: 后记
sections.content_zh:
后记

冯骥才在《传统村落的困境与出路》一文中指出：在进入二十一世纪时，我国自然村总数为363万个，到了2010年，仅仅过去十年，总数锐减为271万个。十年内减少90万个自然村。对于我们这个传统的农耕国家可是个惊天数字。

浙江步入工业文明之后，传统村落急剧消失，工业化地带已经少有传统村落存在，松阳县成了浙江传统村落最后的聚集地之一。从某种程度上来说，松阳县承担着保护浙江传统村落文化的重任。但是，松阳县传统村落的保护状态也不容乐观。

正像全国各地传统村落命运一样，一些古建筑遭受雷击、水灾、火灾、虫蚁等侵袭毁损严重，一些无人居住的老宅处于废弃状态。工业化侵袭、新农村建设、旧村改造中一批传统村落正在遭到破坏，城市化进程造成乡村民俗文化逐渐消失，一些急待修缮的古建筑由于缺乏维修资金进入危房名单。这些凝聚了1800年农业文明历史精华的传统村落的生态链已经非常脆弱，再不加以保护，也许几十年后将从眼前彻底消失。

近年来，松阳县传统村落的价值已经渐渐得到了民间、政府的认可和重视，一群民俗爱好者立足于松阳本土，自发形成了一个民间传统村落保护群体。他们利用文字和相机记录传统村落的建筑、宗族、耕读、商贾、宗教、风水、风俗等文化遗存，已经挖掘、收集、整理出100多个传统村落的文字资料，拍摄了300多个村落的照片，出版了《村居录》、《松古村语》等多部书籍，为传统村落的保护开发利用奠定了基础。目前，传统村落保护已经列入了松阳县委县政府的文化战略，提出了古村复活的口号，制订了保护规划和措施。划定了44个保护村落，石仓七村、界首、山下阳等一些传统村落的修复行动已经启动，全县230余座宗祠中已经有70余座得到了修缮。县史志办收集到600多本族谱，整理出一些家法、家谱和村规民约。提出培育温良恭俭让、克己复礼等传统美德，保护生产、生活、节庆、集市等民俗，保护民间戏剧、祭祀、信仰和各种手工技艺等文化资源。这些实质性的行动标志着松阳县传统村落保护迈出了重要一步，这对于保护浙西南文化历史和建筑史都具探索意义。在社会各界齐心努力下，原本陷入困局的松阳县传统村落保护工作或将走向春天。

此次由松阳县文联编辑、中国文联出版社出版的《江南秘境：松阳传统村落》一书，以文化散文的方式，以村落寻访为主线，图文并茂，将松阳传统村落部分文化遗产呈现在读者面前。然而松阳传统村落精彩纷呈，我们书写和拍摄的也只是极小的精华部分。期待您随着书中文字和照片的引导，看不厌一路的旖旎山水，道不尽一路的乡土文化。我们期待的不是走马观花的喧闹旅游，而是在这些古老的泥墙、砖瓦、石雕、木雕、民俗、物产之中清晰地找到你的精神家园，我们希望这些传统村落的迷人之处能慰藉一颗颠迷连的都市心灵……

本人利用业余时间，断断续续地书写了多年，由于本人学养、视觉、历史观所限，本书难免存在纰漏和主观臆断，希望各位看官予以斧正。在写作过程中，得到了汤光新、叶荣亮、叶永萱、叶坚红、叶平等地方文史专家的帮助，收录了叶高兴、毛进军、郑忠民、阙献荣、吴军等本土摄影家的图片，在此一并感谢！

鲁晓敏
2013年11月于松阳
